name: acpica
desc: OS-independent implementation of the ACPI specification
why: Intel's reference ACPI interpreter lets you explore the firmware tables and bytecode hiding inside every machine.

brief.what_it_is: ACPICA (ACPI Component Architecture) is an OS-independent C implementation of the ACPI specification. Its kernel-side parts are an AML interpreter, a table manager, a namespace manager, a resource manager, fixed and general-purpose event support, and hardware support, plus optional AML disassembler and debugger modules. It also ships user-space tools: the iASL ACPI source compiler and disassembler, AcpiExec (a simulator/executer), acpidump (dumps system ACPI tables to ASCII), acpixtract (the inverse of acpidump), and AcpiHelp. It takes in ACPI firmware tables and AML bytecode, or ASL source for iASL, and produces ASCII table dumps, disassembled source, or compiled AML. The brew executables also include acpibin, acpiexamples and acpisrc, which I did not see described in the pages I read.
brief.why_it_exists: The project describes ACPI as moving power management from the BIOS to the operating system, with the firmware describing the machine in tables that the OS must interpret. ACPICA provides a reference implementation so that OS developers do not have to write that interpreter and table handling from scratch.
brief.how_it_works: ACPICA isolates all operating-system dependencies in a relatively small translation layer called the OS Services Layer, so the bulk of the code stays independent of any single OS. Per the site, a new OS needs no source changes inside ACPICA itself, only the services layer and initialization calls in its startup routine. The components run in both kernel mode and user mode.
brief.install_notes: No brew-specific setup was described. The site says source packages are provided for Microsoft Windows (the Windows package includes Visual C++ project files and ACPI utilities) and for UNIX. There is no stand-alone Linux source package; ACPICA updates for Linux arrive periodically as patches to be merged into the kernel tree. The GitHub repo has a Makefile at the root, but I did not read build instructions, so I cannot say what the build needs beyond ANSI C.
brief.standout: The same ACPICA code runs inside kernels and in user-space tools, and the site says almost every operating system except Windows uses it to enable ACPI. The package also includes an ASL compiler and AcpiExec, a simulator that lets you run firmware bytecode without the target hardware. The site also documents a 'slack mode' that tolerates AML control methods that forget an explicit return, a bug it says Windows masks.
brief.status: unknown. The GitHub page shows about 15,522 commits, 641 stars and 443 forks, but I did not see a last-commit date or a release date. The acpica.org site says ACPICA is 'actively maintained and updated' with releases 'approximately on a monthly to quarterly basis', but its newest news item is dated August 27, 2024 and the news list is otherwise older.
brief.caveats: Dual licensed under BSD-3-Clause or GPL-2.0-only, per the GitHub About panel and the CONTRIBUTING file. No stand-alone Linux source package; Linux support comes as kernel patches. The GitHub URL I was given returned the CONTRIBUTING.md text rather than a README, and the repo file listing shows no README, so the usage details here are thin. The site's feature list says ACPI 5.0 support, while its news says ACPI 6.4 support arrived in 2021, so the spec version coverage is unclear. The site does not mention macOS. The scout note's claim that it lets you explore firmware tables and bytecode is consistent with the tool list, but I saw no usage examples to confirm it.
quotes: ACPICA is actively maintained and updated.
AML stands for ACPI Machine Language. This is a binary pseudo-code format, which the operating system's ACPI AML interpreter parses to discover the machine's properties.
It is a dual license, so your contribution may be included in downstream projects under any of the two alternative licenses.
fetch_log: https://github.com/acpica/acpica: worked, but returned the CONTRIBUTING.md text plus the repo sidebar (About, stars, license), not a README. The file listing shows dev_docs, documents, generate, source, tests and zephyr folders and no README.
https://www.acpica.org: worked; returned the overview, what's included, system requirements, environments, news and FAQ. Some page markup was noisy, but the text was readable.

judge.reason: ACPICA lets you inspect and disassemble your machine’s firmware tables and run ACPI bytecode in a simulator, opening up a hidden layer of everyday computers.

entry.title: ACPICA
entry.tldr: Intel's reference ACPI toolkit: dump your machine's firmware tables, disassemble the AML bytecode inside, and run it in a simulator.
entry.deeper_look:
ACPI is how firmware tells an operating system what the machine is. Instead of the BIOS managing power itself, it hands the OS a set of tables. Some of those tables contain AML, ACPI Machine Language, which the project describes as "a binary pseudo-code format, which the operating system's ACPI AML interpreter parses to discover the machine's properties." Every PC has this bytecode sitting in its firmware.

ACPICA is the reference implementation of the interpreter side. Its kernel-side parts include an AML interpreter, a table manager, a namespace manager, a resource manager and event support. The project says almost every operating system except Windows uses it to enable ACPI. All OS-specific code is isolated in a small translation layer, so the same code runs inside kernels and in user-space tools.

The user-space tools are what make it a door for a curious person. acpidump writes the system's ACPI tables out as ASCII, and acpixtract does the reverse. iASL compiles ASL source to AML and disassembles AML back to source. AcpiExec is a simulator that runs firmware bytecode without the target hardware. AcpiHelp is a lookup aid. The brew formula also installs acpibin, acpiexamples and acpisrc, which the brief does not describe.

The site also documents a 'slack mode' that tolerates AML control methods that forget an explicit return, a bug it says Windows masks. It is a small sign of how much real-world firmware is sloppy.

try_this.what_happens: Lists the options of the ASL compiler and AML disassembler.
Shows how to dump the machine's ACPI tables as ASCII; reading real tables may need elevated privileges or a supported OS.
Shows how to look up ASL and AML terms from the command line.

entry.whats_unique: It is the same interpreter code that real kernels use, packaged with a compiler, disassembler and simulator, so you can read and run firmware bytecode yourself.
entry.caveats: The brief found no README or usage examples, and the site says nothing about macOS, so dumping tables on a Mac may not work and the tools may be most useful on saved table files.
